title: Few-Shot Prompting
description: Show the AI exactly what you want by providing examples — one of the most reliable techniques for consistent output.

data.text: Telling the AI what you want is sometimes less effective than showing it. Few-shot prompting means including 1-3 examples of the desired input-output format in your prompt. This is especially powerful for recurring tasks where you need consistent, predictable output structure.

data.caption: The more examples you provide, the more reliably the AI matches your desired format — especially for unusual or specific output styles
data.definition:
graph TD
  subgraph ZERO ["Zero-shot\n(no examples)"]
    ZI["Instruction only\n'Summarize this'"] --> ZO["Output varies\n(format unpredictable)"]
  end
  subgraph ONE ["One-shot\n(1 example)"]
    OI["Example: 'Great\nexperience!' → Positive\n---\nClassify: 'The\nonboarding was rough'"] --> OO["More likely\nto match format"]
  end
  subgraph FEW ["Few-shot\n(2-3 examples)"]
    FI["3 varied examples\ncovering edge cases"] --> FO["High format consistency\nand robust handling"]
  end

  style ZERO fill:#fff1f0,stroke:#cf222e
  style ONE fill:#fff8e1,stroke:#9a6700
  style FEW fill:#e6ffed,stroke:#1a7f37

rows: Strict formatting, recurring tasks, batch processing

data.title: Feedback classification (few-shot)
data.content:
Classify each customer feedback item as: Positive, Negative, Mixed, or Neutral.

Examples:
"The onboarding was smooth and fast." → Positive
"I waited 3 days for a reply." → Negative
"I received my order." → Neutral
"The product is good but setup took forever." → Mixed

Now classify these:
1. "The product works but the instructions were unclear."
2. "Absolutely love the new dashboard!"
3. "My invoice was wrong twice in a row."

data.title: Tone-matching (one-shot)
data.content:
Write a product description in this style:

Example: "Introducing the Arc — a bag that disappears when you need it and reappears when you don't. Designed for people who hate carrying stuff but can't stop going places.'

Now write one for: [NEW PRODUCT DESCRIPTION]

→ The AI will match the quirky, minimalist brand voice precisely because it has a concrete example to pattern-match against.

data.title: Data extraction template (few-shot)
data.content:
Extract company and funding amount from each sentence. Format as JSON.

Examples:
"Acme Corp raised $5M in Series A." → {"company": "Acme Corp", "amount": "$5M", "round": "Series A"}
"BrightPath secured $12M from Andreessen Horowitz." → {"company": "BrightPath", "amount": "$12M", "round": "unknown"}

Now extract from:
1. "Nimble raised $3.5M in seed funding led by Y Combinator."
2. "DataFlow Inc. closed a $50M Series B round."

rows: Include edge cases in your examples
If you only show clean examples, the AI will fail on messy real-world inputs
Keep example format identical to desired output
The AI will replicate the format exactly — use this to your advantage
Quality of examples matters more than quantity
Vary the examples to cover different sub-cases
Helps AI understand the classification boundary, not just one instance
Save working few-shot prompts as templates
Reuse them for recurring batch tasks without rebuilding each time
Place examples close to the new query
Models pay more attention to the most recent context in the prompt window
Reduces ambiguity and improves parsing for structured tasks

data.title: When to use few-shot
data.text: Use few-shot when you need consistent formatting, a specific tone the AI keeps missing, or when you are processing a batch of similar items. It is especially powerful for turning AI into a reliable extraction or classification engine.

data.title: Key points
points: Examples in your prompt are often more powerful than long instructions
Use 2-3 examples for recurring tasks to get reliable consistency
Few-shot works best for: classification, structured extraction, tone-matching, batch tasks
Include edge cases in examples so the AI handles messy real-world inputs
Save your working few-shot prompts as templates for reuse

data.text: Start with short, copyable templates. Keep examples concise and consistent. Below are beginner-friendly templates you can paste into a prompt and adapt to your domain.

rows:
"Example 1:
Input: 'The onboarding was smooth.'
Output: Positive

Example 2:
Input: 'I waited 3 days for a reply.'
Output: Negative

Now classify:
Input: '[NEW TEXT]'
Output:",

"Example:
Input: 'Acme Corp raised $5M in Series A.'
Output: {"company": "Acme Corp", "amount": "$5M", "round": "Series A"}

Now extract from: '[NEW SENTENCE]'
Output:",

"Example:
Input: 'Product X'
Output: 'Introducing Product X — [quirky one-liner].'

Now write for: '[NEW PRODUCT]'
Output:",

data.text: Combine few-shot with other techniques for stronger results: pair few-shot with chain-of-thought when you want the model to explain its mapping; use self-consistency to sample multiple outputs and vote; use prompt-chaining to break complex tasks into smaller few-shot steps; and add deterministic verification for critical fields.

data.caption: Hybrid workflow: few-shot + CoT + verification
data.definition:
graph TD
  U["User input"] --> F["Few-shot prompt (examples + instruction)"]
  F --> C["Chain-of-thought reasoning (optional)"]
  C --> S["Sample multiple outputs (self-consistency)"]
  S --> V["Automated verification / schema check"]
  V --> R["Final structured output"]

  style U fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style R fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37

data.text: Self-consistency samples multiple outputs (often with higher temperature) and aggregates the final answers (majority vote or confidence-weighted). When combined with few-shot examples that show the desired aggregation format, this approach reduces brittle single-output failures.

rows: Does the output match the exact structure shown in examples?
Critical for downstream parsing and automation
Are labels or extracted values correct?
Does the prompt handle noisy or edge-case inputs?
How long and how expensive is the prompt to run (context length matters)?
Do repeated runs produce consistent outputs?

data.text: Few-shot improves consistency but does not eliminate hallucinations or factual errors. Always validate critical fields with deterministic checks or external data sources before using outputs in production.

Common pitfalls include: overfitting to the examples (model copies examples too literally), exceeding the model's context window with many or long examples, failing to include negative or ambiguous examples which leads to brittle behavior, and hidden biases in examples that propagate to outputs. Few-shot is not a substitute for fine-tuning when you need large-scale, consistent behavior across millions of queries.

For production use: (1) keep examples concise and representative, (2) store prompt templates centrally and version them, (3) run adversarial tests, (4) add lightweight verification (regex, schema validation, lookups), (5) monitor drift and update examples when real inputs change, and (6) log failures for continuous improvement.

data.caption: Production flow for few-shot pipelines
data.definition:
graph TD
  User["Incoming data"] --> P["Apply few-shot prompt"]
  P --> V["Validate output (schema, regex)"]
  V --> A["Auto-accept if valid"]
  V --> H["Human review if invalid or low confidence"]
  H --> DB["Store corrected examples for prompt updates"]

  style User fill:#fff3bf,stroke:#d97706
  style DB fill:#e6f4ff,stroke:#0366d6

data.text: Create a test suite of representative inputs including edge cases and adversarial examples. Measure format adherence, accuracy, and stability. Use automated checks to reject outputs that fail schema validation and route them to human review. Periodically refresh examples based on logged failures.

data.text: When scaling few-shot prompts, balance the number and length of examples against the model's context window. Consider moving rarely changing examples to a short system instruction or using retrieval-augmented prompts for long example sets.

Few-shot prompting is a practical, low-effort way to get consistent, structured outputs from LLMs without fine-tuning. Start with 2–3 high-quality examples, include edge cases, validate outputs, and iterate. Combine few-shot with verification and other prompting techniques for the best results.
